newsitem.title: GAMBIA: Army strongman wins Gambia poll, rival flees.
newsitem.headline: Army strongman wins Gambia poll, rival flees.

text.p: Gambia's Yahya Jammeh has coasted to victory in presidential elections just over two years after taking power in a coup, giving him an emphatic mandate to continue in power as a civilian head of state.
His main rival, lawyer Ousainou Darboe, took refuge in the Senegalese embassy in Banjul along with some family members and political associates, Senegalese officials said.
Final results announced on Friday night by the Provisional Independent Electoral Commission showed Jammeh polled 220,011 votes, or 55.76 percent. Darboe had 141,387 votes, or 35.84 percent.
The voting on Thursday was peaceful and orderly, with 88 percent of some 444,000 registered voters casting ballots.
However, the legal framework for the poll was slammed by critics at home and abroad as meant to ensure Jammeh's victory.
Jammeh banned Gambia's main political parties and experienced politicians linked to founding president Sir Dawda Jawara, who was toppled by Jammeh and accused of corruption.

The Commonwealth and the United Nations denounced the electoral law as grossly flawed and called off plans to send observers for the election. Parliamentary polls are set for December to complete the transition to democracy.
There has been no official explanation for Darboe's action in taking refuge in the embassy, but many officials of his United Democratic Party have spoken of threats from soldiers backing Jammeh.
Asked to comment on Darboe's action, Jammeh told a television interviewer: "I am hearing about this for the first time. You should go and ask him."
Wild celebrations broke out in the streets of the capital Banjul after electoral chief Gabriel Roberts announced the results on television.

Soldiers in uniform were shown on television dancing with Jammeh's ministers at an impromptu state house party, while Jammeh appeared in a flowing gown and dark glasses shaking hands with ministers, cheering women and office staff.

Two other marginal civilian candidates, Amath Bah of the National Reconciliation Party and Sidia Jatta of the People's Democratic Organisation for Independence and Socialism, got 21,759 votes or 5.5 percent and 11,337 votes or 2.9 percent respectively.

Jammeh's win is bound to alarm democracy campaigners in West Africa faced with a new political challenge: coupmakers exploiting the advantage of incumbency to legitimise their rule through the ballot box.
Such elections left political tension in their wake in Niger and Chad.
Jammeh, 31, seized power in a 1994 coup, toppling elected president Sir Dawda Jawara who had ruled the tiny country of one million people since independence from Britain in 1965.

Jammeh resigned from the army last month to contest the elections that he brought forward from 1998 following Western pressure. Western creditors froze aid and some put a temporary ban on their nationals travelling to the tourist haven.
